data_section_full_text:
We conducted individual interviews with 30 practicing audit partners from one Big 4
accounting firm. <sup>8</sup> Participants comprise 14 experienced partners (with a mean of 32.9 years
of audit experience) and 16 newer partners (mean of 15.4 years). Experienced partners
were admitted to the partnership between 1983 and 1993, and the newer partners between
2005 and 2008. <sup>9</sup> While 93 percent of experienced partners interviewed are male, 56 percent
of newer partners interviewed are female. The participants represent a range of geographical locations in the United States and primary industry specializations, which consisted
of manufacturing and services (34 percent); financial services (26 percent); technology
(23 percent); health care (9 percent); and other (9 percent). <sup>10</sup> Obtaining the perspective of
audit partners for this study is valuable for four reasons: (i) their experience enables them
to provide educated and elaborate responses; (ii) they have participated as both guides
and learners; (iii) they have attained the highest rank within the firm and thus have met
standards for performance and conduct; and (iv) they are responsible for setting the “tone
at the top” for each audit engagement. Gaining the perspectives of both newly minted and
more experienced partners provides a variety of generational experiences, enabling a view
of professional practice that spans several decades.

Development of the instrument

We developed the preliminary instrument based on prior literature, as well as insights
from two directors and one senior manager from the firm’s national office. These same
individuals also reviewed our preliminary instrument with minimal revisions suggested.
We then piloted the instrument with a retired partner from a large audit firm and subsequently modified our interview questions for completeness and clarity. The final version of
the instrument consists of ten semi-structured interview questions (with some questions
containing multiple parts) about the current and past status of OTJL in public accounting,

8. A National Director at one Big 4 firm selected the participants based on our criteria (diversity in levels of
experience, gender, current office location, starting office location/country, and industry group), and the
partners’ ability and willingness to participate within the study’s time frame.
9. The responses of newer and more experienced partners to our interview questions are often similar, but
some differences are evident. Relative to more experienced partners, newer partners more frequently note
that emphasis on coaching has increased over time; new staff have a lower level of commitment to the profession (and/or remaining with the firm); seniors have less exposure to technical accounting, as this work
is being more often performed by more experienced auditors; IT enhances flexibility, but reduces human
interaction and coaching; feedback is less effective when not given in real time; and good coaching is
rewarded as a part of the firm’s (annual) evaluation process. Nonetheless, these differences are relative and
both groups generally agree on overall trends. For each quote provided throughout the paper, we provide
a partner reference number and industry affiliation. References leading with an “E” denote experienced
partners and those leading with an “N” denote newer partners.
10. The category of “Manufacturing and Services” includes industrial products, energy, transportation, and
retail. “Financial Services” includes real estate, private equity, investment management, banking, capital
markets and mergers and acquisitions, while “Other” includes oil and gas, not-for profit, and entertainment. Some partners indicated more than one industry specialty over the course of their careers.

and specific factors that advance or hinder learning in this environment. <sup>11</sup> Participants
were also afforded the opportunity to identify additional factors of importance. It is
important to note that the instrument evolved over the course of the interviews (see also
Hirst and Koonce 1996; Cohen, Krishnamoorthy, and Wright 2002; Trompeter and
Wright 2010). After each series of interviews (approximately every three interviews), we
reviewed and reevaluated our questions. Our reevaluation process led us to add subquestions to address common topics that arose during the interviews.


Data collection

Interviews were conducted in late 2008 to early 2009, averaging approximately one hour
in length (ranging from 30 to 100 minutes). We conducted 17 interviews by phone and 13
interviews in person, with two researchers participating in all but one interview. All interviewees gave consent to be recorded by the interviewers. On a rotating basis, one
researcher acted as the primary interviewer, while the other researcher took notes to
ensure retention of data in case of poor audio recording quality or recording failure. We
first established rapport with the partners by discussing the general purpose of our
research and our prior experiences as auditors, and reaffirmed confidentiality. Most partners provided client-specific and personal examples that were both positive and negative
in nature, leading us to believe that their responses were candid. For the few partners
whose responses seemed to be reciting formal firm policy, we asked more probing followup questions in an attempt to elicit more candid responses. We hired professional transcribers to convert the recordings into text. During the data consolidation process, we
reviewed transcripts for accuracy, noting only minor errors in accounting/auditing terminology.

Data analysis


To develop the coding scheme, we independently developed categorizations of responses
for each question. We then compared and refined categories and performed a preliminary
analysis by hand. Next, we uploaded all transcripts into NVivo for formal analysis. <sup>12</sup> Two
authors independently coded each question, with 90 percent intercoder agreement. To
resolve the few disagreements, we referred back to the original transcript for clarification
or support. The remaining author reviewed all coded quotations.
